articleHtml:
By David Vance, Senior Financial Modeler · Last updated: November 27, 2026

The rate you see is not the rate you get

When you search "USD to INR" you see the mid-market rate: the midpoint between the price banks quote to buy and to sell a currency with each other. Retail customers almost never get that rate. Banks, card networks, airport kiosks and transfer apps add a markup, sometimes called a spread, and often a separate fee as well. This tool shows you the mid-market figure so you have a fair benchmark to compare any quote against.

About our rates: rates are sourced from European Central Bank (ECB) and interbank foreign exchange markets and refreshed every daily at 16:00 UTC. They are indicative and for information only; the rate executed by your provider will differ.

Worked example: sending $1,000 to India

All rates in this page are illustrations, not market quotes. Assume the mid-market rate is 1 USD = 85.00 INR. At that rate $1,000 is worth ₹85,000. Now see what different markups do:

Provider markupRate you getRecipient receivesHidden cost
0% (mid-market)85.000₹85,000—
0.5%84.575₹84,575₹425 (≈ $5)
1%84.150₹84,150₹850 (≈ $10)
3%82.450₹82,450₹2,550 (≈ $30)
4.5%81.175₹81,175₹3,825 (≈ $45)

The difference between the best and worst case is ₹3,825 on a single $1,000 transfer. A "zero fee" promotion means nothing if the exchange rate carries a 3% markup.

How to compare any quote in 30 seconds

  1. Look up the mid-market rate right now (use the converter above).
  2. Ask the provider the exact amount the recipient will receive after all fees.
  3. Compute: total cost % = (mid-market value − amount received) ÷ mid-market value.

Fixed fees count too. A $20 flat fee plus a 1% markup on $1,000 costs $30 in total, the same as a "no fee" transfer with a 3% markup. On larger amounts the flat fee matters less; on small amounts it dominates.

Transfer settlement times, clearing networks, and rate locks

When transferring funds overseas via SWIFT or international clearing networks, processing intervals typically range from instantaneous delivery to two or three business days. Specialist digital money transfer services frequently provide a guaranteed exchange-rate lock for 24 to 48 hours while your domestic bank deposit clears. If your chosen provider does not offer a rate lock, your transaction will execute at the prevailing floating market rate when funds arrive, introducing unpredictable currency volatility risk on large remittances or business invoices.

Four common ways people overpay

  • Airport and hotel kiosks. Convenience pricing can put the total cost well above bank rates.
  • Dynamic currency conversion (DCC). When a card terminal or ATM abroad offers to charge you in your home currency, the offered rate usually carries a larger markup than your card network's. Choose to pay in the local currency.
  • Foreign transaction fees. Many cards add a percentage on top of the network rate. Check your card's terms before travelling.
  • Weekend markups. Some providers widen their spreads when markets are closed because they carry more risk. Compare quotes on weekdays if you can.

Should you wait for a better rate?

Exchange rates move on interest rates, inflation data, trade flows and sentiment, and professional forecasters get them wrong often. If you must convert for a known bill, such as tuition or a mortgage payment overseas, a practical approach is to convert part now and part later to average the rate, or ask your provider about a rate alert or forward contract if the amount is large. Trying to time the market with household money is closer to speculation than planning.

Rates for different purposes

  • Remittances: compare effective rates across banks and transfer services. Use the formula above.
  • Travel: a no-foreign-fee card plus local-currency payment is usually cheaper than cash exchanged at a kiosk. Withdraw larger amounts less often if your bank charges per ATM use.
  • Online shopping: check the final charge in your own currency before you pay.
  • Freelancers and exporters: invoice in the currency your costs are in where possible, and compare payout services on the effective rate.

Common mistakes

  • Using the search-engine rate to plan a transfer and being surprised by the result.
  • Comparing fees but not rates.
  • Accepting "pay in your currency" at a foreign terminal.
  • Rounding: a rate of 84.575 versus 84.6 on ₹85,000 changes the outcome by a few rupees per $1,000.

Frequently asked questions

What is the mid-market exchange rate?

It is the midpoint between the buy and sell prices of a currency pair on the wholesale market. It is the fair benchmark, but retail customers rarely receive it.

Why does my bank's rate differ from this converter?

Banks add a markup to the wholesale rate and may also charge fees. Rates also move continuously, so a time difference of even a few minutes can change the figure.

How do I calculate the true cost of a currency transfer?

Subtract the amount the recipient actually receives from the mid-market value of what you sent, then divide by the mid-market value. This includes both the markup and any fixed fees.

Is it cheaper to exchange currency before travelling or abroad?

Often neither airport kiosk is cheap. A card with no foreign transaction fee or a withdrawal at a bank ATM, paid in the local currency, tends to be better. Compare against the mid-market rate.

Methodology and sources

Mid-market conversion = amount × rate. Illustrations on this page use a hypothetical rate of 85.00 for clarity. For consumer guidance on international money transfers see the CFPB's remittance resources. This page is informational, not financial advice. Corrections: support@smartcalclab.com.
